newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-court slams Italy for reading prisoners' mail.
newsitem.headline: Euro-court slams Italy for reading prisoners' mail.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights condemned Italy on Friday for laws allowing guards to censor the mail of two prisoners serving long jail terms for guerrilla crimes.

The court ruled that the government had violated privacy rights of Calogero Diana, a suspected Red Brigades guerrilla sentenced to 27 years in jail in 1981, and of Massimo Domenichini, jailed in 1984 on terrorist charges.

The judges ruled unanimously that the authorities could read prisoners' mail in certain cases, but that Italian laws gave them "too much latitude" by failing to define how long censorship might last or exact reasons for intercepting letters.
Among Domenichini's letters opened were five to his lawyers, also violating his right to prepare a confidential defence, the court ruled.

The court, a branch of the 40-nation Council of Europe whose rulings are binding, did not award either of the two men damages, saying "the judgment constituted in itself just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage".
Rome had argued the two men, transferred to more open prisons in the 1990s, had failed to exhaust appeals in domestic courts before taking the case to Strasbourg.
